Lab 4: Measurement, Reliability, and Measurement Error

Intermediate Quantitative Methods · Week 4

Author

Sebastian Ramirez-Ruiz

Term

Autumn 2026

Welcome! 👋

This week’s seminar was about measurement: how we get from a concept to a number, how we argue that the number is valid, and what happens to our estimates when the number is noisy. Today we turn those ideas into code. The lab has four parts:

  • First, we build a scale from survey items, the way you will for many of the attitudes in your dissertation: reverse-coding, averaging, and checking how well the items hang together.
  • Second, we estimate reliability: test–retest correlations for panel data and agreement between two human coders.
  • Third, we simulate what measurement error does to a regression: in the treatment, in the outcome, in a control, and when the error depends on the treatment.
  • Fourth, we transport an effect from the study population to a new one.

Along the way, we practice the R skills that make this kind of work easy: writing functions, iterating with {purrr}, reshaping with {tidyr}, and operating on many columns at once with across().

Every data set today is simulated. That is the point: when we write the data-generating process ourselves, we know the truth, and we can see exactly when our measures and models recover it.

Packages 📦

# Install these in your CONSOLE if you have not done so yet:
# install.packages(c("tidyverse", "broom", "modelsummary"))

library(tidyverse) # data wrangling and plots; loads {dplyr}, {tidyr}, {purrr}, {ggplot2}
library(broom) # tidy model output
library(modelsummary) # regression tables

Part I: Building a scale 🧱

Our data: trust in institutions 🏛

Many concepts in political science and sociology, such as institutional trust, populist attitudes, or perceived discrimination, are measured with a battery of survey items, each a noisy window onto the same underlying attitude.

We simulate a survey of 1,500 respondents. Each respondent has a latent level of institutional trust (trust_latent), which in real data we would never see. We then generate six 0–10 survey items from it:

Item Question (0 = no trust at all, 10 = complete trust)
trust_parliament How much do you trust the national parliament?
trust_politicians How much do you trust politicians?
trust_parties How much do you trust political parties?
trust_courts How much do you trust the legal system?
trust_police How much do you trust the police?
dont_care “Politicians don’t care what people like me think” (0 = disagree, 10 = agree)

Notice the last item: it is worded in the opposite direction. Agreeing means less trust. Reverse-worded items are common in surveys because they reduce “yea-saying”, but they have to be reverse-coded before we combine them with the others.

We also simulate an outcome: an index of compliance with public health rules (higher = more compliant). In our simulated world, trust causes compliance, and nothing else confounds the relationship.

We write a small function that turns the latent trait into a 0–10 item. Each item gets its own loading (how strongly it reflects trust) and its own noise:

make_item <- function(latent, loading, noise_sd = 1.5) {
  raw <- 5 + 2 * loading * latent + rnorm(length(latent), 0, noise_sd)
  raw <- round(raw) # survey answers are whole numbers
  pmin(pmax(raw, 0), 10) # keep them inside the 0-10 scale
}

pmax(raw, 0) replaces every value below 0 with 0, and pmin(..., 10) every value above 10 with 10. They work element by element on whole vectors, which is what we need here.

n <- 1500

survey <- tibble::tibble(
  id = 1:n,
  trust_latent = rnorm(n), # the attitude we care about (unobservable!)
  trust_parliament = make_item(trust_latent, loading = 0.9),
  trust_politicians = make_item(trust_latent, loading = 0.9),
  trust_parties = make_item(trust_latent, loading = 0.8),
  trust_courts = make_item(trust_latent, loading = 0.7),
  trust_police = make_item(trust_latent, loading = 0.5),
  dont_care = make_item(-trust_latent, loading = 0.8), # reverse-worded
  compliance = 6 + 1 * trust_latent + rnorm(n, 0, 2) # an index, higher = more compliant
)

head(survey)

Looking at many items at once: tidyr::pivot_longer() 🔄

To plot all six items side by side, we need the data in long format: one row per respondent and item. Lab 1 introduced pivot_longer(); this is a typical use.

items_long <- survey %>%
  dplyr::select(id, trust_parliament:dont_care) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(cols = -id, names_to = "item", values_to = "answer")

head(items_long)
ggplot(items_long, aes(x = answer)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "#2f1a61") +
  facet_wrap(~ item) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Answer (0-10)", y = "Number of respondents")

Do the items hang together? Correlations 🔗

If the items measure the same thing, they should be positively correlated. cor() on a data frame of numeric columns returns the full correlation matrix:

item_cors <- survey %>%
  dplyr::select(trust_parliament:dont_care) %>%
  cor()

round(item_cors, 2)
                  trust_parliament trust_politicians trust_parties trust_courts
trust_parliament              1.00              0.56          0.54         0.52
trust_politicians             0.56              1.00          0.51         0.52
trust_parties                 0.54              0.51          1.00         0.48
trust_courts                  0.52              0.52          0.48         1.00
trust_police                  0.43              0.42          0.40         0.36
dont_care                    -0.56             -0.57         -0.50        -0.48
                  trust_police dont_care
trust_parliament          0.43     -0.56
trust_politicians         0.42     -0.57
trust_parties             0.40     -0.50
trust_courts              0.36     -0.48
trust_police              1.00     -0.42
dont_care                -0.42      1.00

A matrix of numbers is hard to read. A heat map is easier. We turn the matrix into a data frame (as.data.frame()), keep the row names as a column (tibble::rownames_to_column()), and pivot it longer:

item_cors %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column("item_1") %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-item_1, names_to = "item_2", values_to = "r") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = item_1, y = item_2, fill = r)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(r, 2)), size = 3.5) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#cc0065", mid = "white", high = "#2f1a61", limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Correlation")

Activity 💡

  1. Which item stands out in the correlation matrix, and why?
  2. Which of the five trust items is the weakest indicator of institutional trust? Can you think of a substantive reason why that item might behave differently in a real survey?
➨ Click for Answer 🔓
  1. dont_care correlates negatively with every other item, because it is worded in the opposite direction. That is expected, and it is why we must reverse-code it.
  2. trust_police has the weakest correlations: in our simulation it has the smallest loading (0.5). In real surveys, trust in the police and the courts often behaves differently from trust in political institutions: they are sometimes seen as “order” institutions rather than partisan ones. A weak item is a signal to ask whether it measures the same systematized concept (Adcock & Collier) as the rest.

Reverse-coding and averaging with across() 🔁

Reverse-coding a 0–10 item means mapping 0 → 10, 1 → 9, …, 10 → 0: 10 - x.

Then we build the scale: each respondent’s average across the six items. dplyr::across() lets us apply the same operation to several columns at once, and rowMeans() averages across columns, row by row:

survey <- survey %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    dont_care_r = 10 - dont_care, # reverse-coded
    trust_scale = rowMeans(dplyr::across(c(trust_parliament:trust_police, dont_care_r)))
  )

survey %>%
  dplyr::select(id, trust_parliament, dont_care, dont_care_r, trust_scale) %>%
  head()

⚠️ Always check reverse-coding with a quick table or correlation: cor(survey$dont_care, survey$dont_care_r) should be exactly −1. Forgetting to reverse an item, or reversing one twice, is one of the most common (and least visible) errors in published scales.

Cronbach’s α by hand ✍️

In the seminar we defined reliability as the share of the variance in a measure that is true signal. With a multi-item scale, the most common estimate of the reliability of the average is Cronbach’s α:

\[\alpha = \frac{k}{k - 1}\left(1 - \frac{\sum_{j=1}^{k} \text{Var}(\text{item}_j)}{\text{Var}(\text{sum of items})}\right)\]

where \(k\) is the number of items. The intuition: if the items share a lot of signal, the variance of their sum is much larger than the sum of their separate variances (because the covariances add up), and α is close to 1.

Let’s write it as a function that takes a data frame of items:

cronbach_alpha <- function(items) {
  k <- ncol(items)
  item_variances <- purrr::map_dbl(items, var) # variance of each column
  total_variance <- var(rowSums(items)) # variance of the sum score
  (k / (k - 1)) * (1 - sum(item_variances) / total_variance)
}

purrr::map_dbl(items, var) applies var() to every column of the data frame (a data frame is a list of columns) and returns a numeric vector.

Always test a new function on a case where you know the answer. Five identical items are perfectly reliable, so α should be 1:

x <- rnorm(100)
cronbach_alpha(tibble::tibble(a = x, b = x, c = x, d = x, e = x))
[1] 1

Now on our scale:

survey %>%
  dplyr::select(trust_parliament:trust_police, dont_care_r) %>%
  cronbach_alpha()
[1] 0.8512383

Activity 💡

  1. Compute α for the six items without reverse-coding dont_care (use dont_care instead of dont_care_r). What happens?
  2. Compute α for only the three most political items (trust_parliament, trust_politicians, trust_parties). Is it higher or lower than for six items? Why might that be?
  3. Bonus: write a loop with purrr::map_dbl() that computes α for the scale dropping one item at a time (“α if item deleted”). Which item would you consider dropping, and should you?
➨ Click for Answer 🔓 
# 1. forgetting to reverse-code
survey %>%
  dplyr::select(trust_parliament:trust_police, dont_care) %>%
  cronbach_alpha()
[1] 0.4962689
# 2. three political items only
survey %>%
  dplyr::select(trust_parliament, trust_politicians, trust_parties) %>%
  cronbach_alpha()
[1] 0.7769337
# 3. alpha if item deleted
scale_items <- c("trust_parliament", "trust_politicians", "trust_parties",
                 "trust_courts", "trust_police", "dont_care_r")

purrr::map_dbl(scale_items, \(item) {
  survey %>%
    dplyr::select(dplyr::all_of(setdiff(scale_items, item))) %>%
    cronbach_alpha()
}) %>%
  setNames(scale_items) %>%
  round(3)
 trust_parliament trust_politicians     trust_parties      trust_courts 
            0.815             0.817             0.827             0.830 
     trust_police       dont_care_r 
            0.847             0.820
  1. α collapses: the reversed item cancels out part of the shared variance instead of adding to it. A low α is often a coding mistake rather than a bad scale.
  2. α is somewhat lower with three items, even though they are the strongest ones. α grows with the number of items (Spearman–Brown, as in the seminar): more items, more averaging out of noise.
  3. Dropping trust_police barely changes α, and might even raise it slightly. Whether you should drop it is a content validity question, not a statistical one: does your systematized concept of institutional trust include order institutions? Dropping items after looking at the results is one of the questionable measurement practices in Flake & Fried (2020), unless you report it and justify it.

⚠️ Cronbach’s α assumes that all items measure the construct equally well (equal loadings). Ours don’t, so α is a lower bound. Next week we will estimate a model of the construct and compute a better coefficient (McDonald’s ω). If you want to check your α against a package, psych::alpha() reports α plus item statistics.

Part II: Estimating reliability 🎯

Test–retest: the same question, twice 🔁

In a panel survey, the same people answer the same question in several waves. If the attitude itself is stable, the correlation between waves estimates the reliability of the question.

We simulate left–right self-placement (0–10) for 1,000 panel respondents in two waves. Ideology is stable between the waves; only the answers are noisy:

panel <- tibble::tibble(
  ideology = rnorm(1000), # stable latent ideology
  lr_wave1 = pmin(pmax(round(5 + 2 * ideology + rnorm(1000, 0, 1.4)), 0), 10),
  lr_wave2 = pmin(pmax(round(5 + 2 * ideology + rnorm(1000, 0, 1.4)), 0), 10)
)

cor(panel$lr_wave1, panel$lr_wave2)
[1] 0.6272192

About two-thirds of the variance in a single answer is signal. A third is noise: answers that would change if we asked again tomorrow.

Inter-coder reliability: two humans, one codebook 🧑‍🤝‍🧑

Many political science data sets are hand-coded: protest events from newspapers, manifesto sentences, populist rhetoric in speeches. A standard check is to have two coders classify the same documents and compare.

We simulate 400 parliamentary speeches, 30% of which are truly populist. Each coder classifies each speech correctly 90% of the time:

n_speeches <- 400

speeches <- tibble::tibble(
  speech_id = 1:n_speeches,
  populist = rbinom(n_speeches, size = 1, prob = 0.3), # the truth
  coder_a = dplyr::if_else(runif(n_speeches) < 0.9, populist, 1L - populist),
  coder_b = dplyr::if_else(runif(n_speeches) < 0.9, populist, 1L - populist)
)

head(speeches)

runif(n) draws numbers between 0 and 1; runif(n) < 0.9 is TRUE for about 90% of the speeches, where the coder gets it right. Otherwise, 1L - populist flips the code.

The simplest summary is percent agreement:

mean(speeches$coder_a == speeches$coder_b)
[1] 0.7925

But some agreement happens by chance: two coders who both said “not populist” to everything would still agree on 70% of the speeches. Cohen’s κ corrects for this:

\[\kappa = \frac{p_o - p_e}{1 - p_e}\]

where \(p_o\) is the observed agreement and \(p_e\) the agreement we would expect by chance, given how often each coder uses each code.

cohen_kappa <- function(a, b) {
  p_o <- mean(a == b)
  p_e <- mean(a == 1) * mean(b == 1) + mean(a == 0) * mean(b == 0)
  (p_o - p_e) / (1 - p_e)
}

cohen_kappa(speeches$coder_a, speeches$coder_b)
[1] 0.5360796

Activity 💡

Populist speeches are rare in many parliaments. Write a function simulate_coding(prevalence, accuracy = 0.9, n = 400) that simulates two coders as above and returns a one-row tibble with the prevalence, percent agreement, and κ. Then use purrr::map() and purrr::list_rbind() to run it for prevalences of 0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.3, and 0.5.

What happens to percent agreement and to κ as populist speeches get rarer? Which one would you report?

➨ Click for Answer 🔓 
simulate_coding <- function(prevalence, accuracy = 0.9, n = 400) {
  truth <- rbinom(n, size = 1, prob = prevalence)
  a <- dplyr::if_else(runif(n) < accuracy, truth, 1L - truth)
  b <- dplyr::if_else(runif(n) < accuracy, truth, 1L - truth)
  tibble::tibble(prevalence = prevalence,
                 agreement = mean(a == b),
                 kappa = cohen_kappa(a, b))
}

coding_results <- c(0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.3, 0.5) %>%
  purrr::map(simulate_coding) %>%
  purrr::list_rbind()

coding_results
coding_results %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(agreement, kappa), names_to = "statistic", values_to = "value") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = prevalence, y = value, color = statistic)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("agreement" = "#2f1a61", "kappa" = "#cc0065")) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Share of speeches that are truly populist", y = NULL, color = NULL)

The coders are equally good in every scenario (90% accurate), and percent agreement barely moves. But κ falls sharply when the category is rare: most of the agreement is two coders saying “not populist” to speeches that obviously aren’t, which is easy and tells us little. Report κ (or Krippendorff’s α, which generalizes it to more coders and missing codes), and always report how common each category is.

Part III: What measurement error does to a regression 🔬

In the seminar we drew measurement error as another node in the DAG: we analyze \(D^*\) and \(Y^*\), not \(D\) and \(Y\). Now we simulate each case and watch what happens to \(\hat\beta\).

Error in the treatment: attenuation 📉

Let’s go back to our survey. In our simulated world, a 1-SD increase in true trust raises compliance by 1 point. Let’s see what three researchers would find:

  • a researcher with superpowers who observes trust_latent (impossible in real life),
  • a researcher with a single item (trust_parliament), and
  • a researcher with the six-item scale (trust_scale).

To compare the coefficients, we put all three predictors on the same scale (standard deviations) with scale():

models_trust <- list(
  "True trust (superpowers)" = lm(compliance ~ scale(trust_latent), data = survey),
  "Single item" = lm(compliance ~ scale(trust_parliament), data = survey),
  "Six-item scale" = lm(compliance ~ scale(trust_scale), data = survey)
)

modelsummary::modelsummary(
  models_trust,
  coef_rename = function(x) dplyr::if_else(x == "(Intercept)", x, "Trust (1 SD)"),
  gof_map = c("nobs", "r.squared")
)
True trust (superpowers) Single item Six-item scale
(Intercept) 6.015 6.015 6.015
(0.053) (0.055) (0.054)
Trust (1 SD) 0.963 0.719 0.886
(0.053) (0.055) (0.054)
Num.Obs. 1500 1500 1500
R2 0.182 0.101 0.154

The single item understates the effect of trust. The scale does better, because averaging six items cancels out much of the noise. That is the attenuation from the seminar: \(\text{plim}\,\hat\beta = \rho \cdot \beta\).

(With standardized predictors the attenuation factor is \(\sqrt{\rho}\) rather than \(\rho\), but the lesson is the same: the noisier the measure, the smaller the estimate.)

A simulation function for attenuation ⚙️

To see the formula at work, we write a function that simulates one study for a given reliability and returns the estimated slope. We set the error variance so that the reliability is exactly what we ask for:

\[\rho = \frac{\text{Var}(D)}{\text{Var}(D) + \text{Var}(e)} = \frac{1}{1 + \sigma_e^2} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \sigma_e = \sqrt{\frac{1 - \rho}{\rho}}\]

attenuation_sim <- function(reliability, beta = 1, n = 2000) {
  d <- rnorm(n) # true treatment, variance 1
  e <- rnorm(n, 0, sqrt((1 - reliability) / reliability)) # measurement error
  d_star <- d + e # what we observe
  y <- beta * d + rnorm(n) # the outcome depends on the TRUE treatment

  tibble::tibble(reliability = reliability,
                 estimate = coef(lm(y ~ d_star))[["d_star"]])
}

attenuation_sim(reliability = 0.5)

Now we iterate over many reliabilities with purrr::map() and stack the results with purrr::list_rbind():

attenuation_results <- seq(0.1, 1, by = 0.1) %>%
  purrr::map(attenuation_sim) %>%
  purrr::list_rbind()

attenuation_results
ggplot(attenuation_results, aes(x = reliability, y = estimate)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, color = "#2f1a61") +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "#cc0065") +
  annotate("text", x = 0.12, y = 1.05, label = "true effect = 1", hjust = 0, color = "#2f1a61") +
  annotate("text", x = 0.55, y = 0.45, label = "reliability x true effect", hjust = 0, color = "grey40") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Reliability of the measured treatment", y = "Estimated effect")

The estimates sit on the dashed line: the estimated effect is the true effect times the reliability.

Activity 💡

The political science example from the seminar: political interest (the treatment) and turnout. Suppose a single interest item has a reliability of 0.6 and a well-measured education variable has a reliability of 0.95. In truth, both have the same effect on participation (β = 0.5).

Use attenuation_sim() to estimate both effects. A reviewer asks you which matters more for participation, interest or education. What would the estimates suggest, and why is that conclusion wrong?

➨ Click for Answer 🔓 
dplyr::bind_rows(
  attenuation_sim(reliability = 0.6, beta = 0.5) %>% dplyr::mutate(variable = "Political interest"),
  attenuation_sim(reliability = 0.95, beta = 0.5) %>% dplyr::mutate(variable = "Education")
)

Education looks almost twice as important as interest, but the true effects are identical. The difference is entirely in how well each variable is measured. Comparing coefficients across predictors measured with different reliability is a rigged horse race.

Error in the outcome: noise, not bias 🌫

Random error in the outcome behaves differently. We repeat one study 500 times with a clean outcome and 500 times with a noisy one, and look at the distribution of estimates.

purrr::map_dbl(1:500, \(i) ...) runs the code inside 500 times and returns the 500 numbers. The i is just a counter; we don’t use it.

one_study <- function(outcome_noise_sd, n = 300, beta = 0.5) {
  d <- rnorm(n)
  y <- beta * d + rnorm(n)
  y_star <- y + rnorm(n, 0, outcome_noise_sd) # noisy outcome
  coef(lm(y_star ~ d))[["d"]]
}

outcome_error <- tibble::tibble(
  clean = purrr::map_dbl(1:500, \(i) one_study(outcome_noise_sd = 0)),
  noisy = purrr::map_dbl(1:500, \(i) one_study(outcome_noise_sd = 2))
) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "outcome", values_to = "estimate")

outcome_error %>%
  dplyr::group_by(outcome) %>%
  dplyr::summarize(mean_estimate = mean(estimate), sd_estimate = sd(estimate))
ggplot(outcome_error, aes(x = estimate, fill = outcome)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.5, color = "#2f1a61") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("clean" = "#2f1a61", "noisy" = "#cc0065")) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Estimated effect (true effect = 0.5)", y = "Density", fill = "Outcome")

Both distributions are centered on the truth: no bias. The noisy outcome makes estimates more spread out, so our confidence intervals will be wider and our studies less powerful.

Error in a control: residual confounding 🧩

The question from Labs 2 and 3: does a university degree make people more positive about immigration? Family background drives both. Real surveys rarely measure family background well. A common proxy in comparative surveys is: “How many books were there in your home when you were 14?”

We simulate the world, and create the noisy proxy with cut(), which turns a continuous variable into ordered categories:

n <- 5000

edu_df <- tibble::tibble(
  background = rnorm(n), # true family background (unobserved)
  books = cut(background + rnorm(n, 0, 1), # a noisy, coarse proxy
              breaks = c(-Inf, -1, -0.3, 0.3, 1, Inf),
              labels = c("0-10", "11-25", "26-100", "101-200", "200+")),
  degree = rbinom(n, size = 1, prob = plogis(-0.3 + 1.2 * background)),
  immigration = 5 + 1 * degree + 1.5 * background + rnorm(n, 0, 2) # true effect of degree = 1
)

dplyr::count(edu_df, books)
models_edu <- list(
  "No control" = lm(immigration ~ degree, data = edu_df),
  "Books at home" = lm(immigration ~ degree + books, data = edu_df),
  "True background (superpowers)" = lm(immigration ~ degree + background, data = edu_df)
)

modelsummary::modelsummary(models_edu, coef_map = c("degree" = "University degree"),
                           gof_map = c("nobs", "r.squared"))
No control Books at home True background (superpowers)
University degree 2.485 1.961 1.015
(0.068) (0.067) (0.063)
Num.Obs. 5000 5000 5000
R2 0.213 0.304 0.466

Controlling for the books proxy closes part of the backdoor path. The remaining bias has the same sign as the original confounding. Only the researcher with superpowers, who controls for the true background, recovers the effect of 1.

Activity 💡

  1. Make the proxy better: change the noise inside cut() from rnorm(n, 0, 1) to rnorm(n, 0, 0.3). What happens to the estimate in the “Books at home” model?
  2. Make it finer: instead of five categories, control for the continuous background + rnorm(n, 0, 1) directly. Does that help as much as reducing the noise?
➨ Click for Answer 🔓 
edu_df <- edu_df %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    books_better = cut(background + rnorm(n, 0, 0.3),
                       breaks = c(-Inf, -1, -0.3, 0.3, 1, Inf)),
    proxy_continuous = background + rnorm(n, 0, 1)
  )

modelsummary::modelsummary(
  list("Better proxy" = lm(immigration ~ degree + books_better, data = edu_df),
       "Continuous noisy proxy" = lm(immigration ~ degree + proxy_continuous, data = edu_df)),
  coef_map = c("degree" = "University degree"), gof_map = c("nobs")
)
Better proxy Continuous noisy proxy
University degree 1.206 1.843
(0.065) (0.067)
Num.Obs. 5000 5000
  1. The estimate moves much closer to 1: less noise in the confounder, less residual confounding.
  2. Keeping the proxy continuous helps a little, but it is still noisy, so a good part of the bias remains. The reliability of the control matters more than its format. “We controlled for X” is only as good as the measure of X.

Differential error: when the treatment changes the answer 🗳

The last case from the seminar: a get-out-the-vote experiment. Half the sample is randomly called and encouraged to vote. Being called raises the probability of voting from 45% to 48%: a true effect of 3 percentage points.

We can measure turnout in two ways: validated turnout from official voter records, or self-reported turnout (“Did you vote?”). Some people who did not vote say they did, and people who were just called by a campaign feel more pressure to say yes:

n <- 20000

gotv <- tibble::tibble(
  called = rbinom(n, size = 1, prob = 0.5), # random assignment
  voted = rbinom(n, size = 1, prob = 0.45 + 0.03 * called), # validated turnout
  # non-voters over-report: 20% in control, 30% among those called
  overreport = rbinom(n, size = 1, prob = dplyr::if_else(called == 1, 0.30, 0.20)),
  says_voted = dplyr::if_else(voted == 1, 1L, overreport) # self-reported turnout
)

gotv %>%
  dplyr::group_by(called) %>%
  dplyr::summarize(validated = mean(voted), self_reported = mean(says_voted))

rbinom() accepts a vector of probabilities, one per person, which is how we give the called and the not-called different chances of over-reporting.

modelsummary::modelsummary(
  list("Validated turnout" = lm(voted ~ called, data = gotv),
       "Self-reported turnout" = lm(says_voted ~ called, data = gotv)),
  coef_map = c("called" = "Called (treatment)"), gof_map = c("nobs")
)
Validated turnout Self-reported turnout
Called (treatment) 0.022 0.074
(0.007) (0.007)
Num.Obs. 20000 20000

The self-reported estimate is more than twice the true effect, even though treatment was randomized. Randomization protects the comparison between groups, not the measurement of the outcome. Part of the “effect” of the call is an effect on what people say.

Activity 💡

Suppose over-reporting is the same in both groups: 25% of non-voters say they voted, whether they were called or not. Change the simulation and re-estimate. Is the self-reported estimate still biased? In which direction?

➨ Click for Answer 🔓 
gotv <- gotv %>%
  dplyr::mutate(overreport_equal = rbinom(n, size = 1, prob = 0.25),
                says_voted_equal = dplyr::if_else(voted == 1, 1L, overreport_equal))

coef(lm(says_voted_equal ~ called, data = gotv))[["called"]]
[1] 0.01297179

Now the estimate is smaller than 3 points: in expectation 3 × (1 − 0.25) ≈ 2.25 points (your number will bounce around that because of sampling noise). With a binary outcome, even nondifferential misreporting biases the difference in proportions toward zero, because some of the non-voters the call failed to mobilize are counted as voters anyway. Differential misreporting can push the estimate in either direction. Validated outcomes avoid both problems.

Part IV: Transporting an effect 🚲

The seminar’s last part asked: does the finding travel? If we know which variables modify the effect, we can move an estimate from the study population to a target population:

\[\text{PATE} = \sum_x \tau(x) \, P_{\text{target}}(X = x)\]

We simulate a study of protected bike lanes in a city where most commutes are short. The effect of a lane on the probability of cycling to work depends on commute distance:

n <- 20000

bike_study <- tibble::tibble(
  distance = sample(c("< 3 km", "3-8 km", "> 8 km"), n, replace = TRUE,
                    prob = c(0.5, 0.4, 0.1)), # the study city's commutes
  lane = rbinom(n, size = 1, prob = 0.5), # randomized lane access
  effect = dplyr::case_when(distance == "< 3 km" ~ 0.10,
                            distance == "3-8 km" ~ 0.06,
                            distance == "> 8 km" ~ 0.01),
  cycles = rbinom(n, size = 1, prob = 0.2 + effect * lane)
)

Step 1: estimate the effect within each distance group (the conditional average treatment effects):

cates <- bike_study %>%
  dplyr::group_by(distance) %>%
  dplyr::summarize(cate = mean(cycles[lane == 1]) - mean(cycles[lane == 0]),
                   study_share = dplyr::n() / nrow(bike_study))

cates

Step 2: bring in the target city’s distribution of commutes, where long commutes are more common, and join it to the estimates:

target_city <- tibble::tibble(distance = c("< 3 km", "3-8 km", "> 8 km"),
                              target_share = c(0.3, 0.4, 0.3))

cates <- dplyr::left_join(cates, target_city, by = "distance")
cates

Step 3: reweight:

cates %>%
  dplyr::summarize(sate = weighted.mean(cate, study_share),
                   pate_target = weighted.mean(cate, target_share))

The lane works in both cities, but the effect we should expect in the target city is smaller, because more of its residents have long commutes, for whom a lane changes little.

⚠️ Reweighting only works if (1) we know the effect modifiers, (2) they are measured the same way in both places, and (3) every type of person in the target also exists in the study (overlap). If the target city has hills and the study city has none, no reweighting by distance will fix it.

Wrap-up 🎁

  • A scale averages several noisy items: reverse-code first, check the correlations, and report α (better: ω, next week). Dropping items after seeing the results is a questionable measurement practice unless you report it.
  • Reliability can be estimated from repeated measurements (test–retest), several coders (κ, not raw agreement), or several items (α).
  • Random error in the treatment attenuates its effect, and makes better-measured variables win horse races. Random error in the outcome adds noise, not bias. Error in a control leaves residual confounding. Differential error, even in a randomized experiment, can bias in any direction.
  • Effects can be transported by reweighting effect modifiers, under strong assumptions.
  • R skills from today: writing and testing functions, purrr::map() / map_dbl() + list_rbind(), tidyr::pivot_longer(), dplyr::across() with rowMeans(), cut(), and weighted.mean().
